lesson.title: No Kings, Just Consensus: Who Actually Writes Internet Protocols
lesson.summary: The IETF is the open, volunteer-driven community that develops and maintains the internet's core protocols, publishing its work as RFCs and favoring rough consensus and working code over top-down authority.
lesson.body:
The Internet Engineering Task Force, or IETF, is the community of engineers who develop and maintain the protocols that make the internet function, and its output is published as the RFC documents covered in an earlier chapter. It has no formal membership and charges no dues. Anyone who wants to participate can join a mailing list, comment on a draft, or show up to one of the three in-person meetings the IETF holds each year at rotating locations around the world, and in practice a great deal of the real work happens asynchronously between meetings on those mailing lists.

Work is organized into working groups, each focused on a specific topic such as routing, security, or a particular application protocol, and working groups are grouped further into areas, each overseen by area directors who together form the Internet Engineering Steering Group, or IESG, which has final say on whether a document is ready to be published as an RFC. The IETF's guiding philosophy is often summarized in a phrase attributed to early Internet Architecture Board member David Clark: "rough consensus and running code." That means a proposal advances not because a single authority approves it or because every participant unanimously agrees, but because the working group has reached broad agreement and, ideally, someone has actually built and tested an implementation that proves the design works in practice rather than just on paper.

Watching a protocol travel from idea to RFC shows the process concretely. An engineer or small group writes an Internet-Draft, a working document that is explicitly temporary and expires after a matter of months unless it is revised. The draft circulates for review and argument on the relevant working group's mailing list and at meetings, often for months or years, going through repeated revisions as implementers report problems and edge cases nobody had considered. HTTP/2 followed exactly this path through the IETF's HTTPBIS working group before being published as RFC 7540 in 2015, and its successor HTTP/3, built on the QUIC transport protocol, went through the same kind of extended review before becoming RFC 9114 in 2022.

This chapter is really where the Protocol and RFC Document chapters converge. A protocol needs precise, written rules covering syntax, semantics, and timing, and the RFC is the document format used to publish those rules, but neither of those things explains who actually writes them and decides when they are ready. The IETF is that body, at least for the specific protocols that run the internet itself. It is worth contrasting this with IEEE, covered in the previous chapter, which standardizes the physical and link-layer hardware underneath internet protocols through a more traditional professional-association structure, while the IETF focuses on the internet layer and above.

Because the IETF's process is open to anyone with technical expertise to contribute and rewards working implementations over institutional rank, no single company or government has ever needed to grant permission for the internet's protocols to spread worldwide. That openness is a large part of why the same TCP/IP protocol suite, defined and refined through this same process for decades, still underlies networks on every continent today.
